signatureModule.title: The Turn Ledger: Three Counterpoints
signatureModule.intro: Before adding another sentence, decide what the reply must change. The ledger rejects the idea that longer turns are automatically better.

items.label: Counterpoint 1
items.title: Dialogue is not decoration
items.bodyMarkdown: Choose a line when it changes what one role lets another role know, question, accept, or resist in the current moment.

items.label: Counterpoint 2
items.title: Action is not a summary
items.bodyMarkdown: Choose a small move when it changes one observable detail while leaving the central consequence for the next turn.

items.label: Counterpoint 3
items.title: Both formats need separate jobs
items.bodyMarkdown: Pair action and dialogue only when the move changes the situation and the line makes the relationship pressure clearer.

title: AI Roleplay Dialogue vs Action: Choose the Next Turn
metaDescription: Choose dialogue, action, or both in an AI roleplay turn with a simple ledger for relationship, situation, and an open pressure.
h1: AI Roleplay Dialogue vs Action: What Should Change Next?
heroMarkdown: The hard part of an AI roleplay reply is often deciding what needs to change. Dialogue shifts a relationship; action alters the immediate situation. Use both only when each has a separate job. The Turn Ledger keeps one response focused and answerable. When a story-led roleplay experience fits, use the attributed CTA intentionally; it opens the approved destination in a new tab.

sections.heading: Name the change before choosing the format
sections.bodyMarkdown: A turn does not need more decoration just because it feels quiet. First ask what must be different after this reply. If the role needs to reveal, refuse, reassure, or test another person, dialogue is usually the useful change. If the room, object, distance, evidence, or immediate risk needs to move, an action is usually the useful change. If both a relationship and a situation need to move together, pair one small action with one line. This is a decision tool, not a guarantee about how any system will answer. Its purpose is to stop a response from becoming a recap with no new job for the next turn.

sections.heading: Read the three columns in the Turn Ledger
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Relationship — choose dialogue.** Use a line when the important change is what one role lets another role know, question, accept, or resist. Keep the line attached to the present moment rather than a full history.

**Situation — choose action.** Use an action when a visible detail must change: a document is moved, a door is checked, a cup is set down, or a distance is created. Let the move be small enough that another turn can react.

**Open pressure — choose both only when needed.** Pair an action and a line when the move makes the relationship question sharper. For example, an original role folds an unsigned note and asks, “Who else saw this?” The fold changes the situation; the question creates pressure.

Do not add both formats merely to make a reply longer. The ledger is useful when each part has a different job.

sections.heading: Test one small paired turn
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Imagine an original scene: a chosen role finds a lantern burning in an otherwise empty archive. Dialogue only might ask, “Did someone leave this for me?” That changes the relationship by inviting an answer, but the situation stays still. Action only might be: *I shield the flame and look beneath the desk.* That changes the situation, but it gives no clear interpersonal pressure.

A paired turn can be smaller than a paragraph: *I move the lantern away from the papers and keep my hand near the drawer.* “If you expected me, say so before I open this.” The action protects something immediate; the line makes the next response choose a position. The archive, lantern, note, and roles are original generic craft material, not a supplied story, a promise, or a borrowed fictional setting.

sections.heading: Send one open pressure, then stop
sections.bodyMarkdown:
- Check the **relationship** column: did a line give another role something specific to answer?

- Check the **situation** column: did an action create one observable change?

- Check the **open pressure** column: can the next turn respond without a separate plot?

Keep only the format that has a job. If the exchange is flat, use the related scene-recovery guide.

faqs.question: When should I use dialogue instead of action in AI roleplay?
faqs.answerMarkdown: Use dialogue when the needed change is relational: a role needs to ask, reveal, refuse, reassure, or test another person. Keep the line tied to one present detail so it gives the next turn a precise response job.

faqs.question: Should every AI roleplay reply include dialogue and action?
faqs.answerMarkdown: No. Pair them only when one small action changes the immediate situation and one line changes the relationship question. A shorter single-format reply is stronger when only one of those changes is needed.

faqs.question: Does choosing a turn form unlock any particular product behavior?
faqs.answerMarkdown: No. The ledger is writing advice. Its only product context is a story-led voice cosplay and roleplay direction in which an existing plot and an available character perspective frame participation. It says nothing about access, individual plots, technical implementation, response characteristics, or results.
